https://www.irishdentist.ie/grandmas-gol.text: Politics July 19, 2026 Grandma’s gold is worth a fortune: the wealth hidden in Italian homes The big bankers on Wall Street spend their days interrogating algorithms as intricate as a charade. Global financial strategists chase artificial intelligence, supercomputers and mysterious market movements. To power his gigantic data centers, Jeff Bezos even goes hunting for copper underground in Arizona, with the spirit of a Klondike gold prospector wearing the helmet of a technological entrepreneur. In Italy, however, the nation’s sovereign wealth fund, the one that preserves the country’s wealth, is within reach. You don’t need to dig mountains, you don’t need drills, you don’t even need an ultra-fast internet connection. Just open the dresser drawer. Yes, exactly that. The sacred place where mismatched socks, old supermarket receipts, faded photographs and, often, a small forgotten heritage coexist: the grandmother’s necklace, the baptism bracelet, the brooch given by the aunt, the ring preserved in a velvet box now worn out by time. A treasure which according to estimates, the reliability of which is difficult to verify, could be worth 150 billion. For years we looked at him with a mixture of tenderness and sufficiency. Objects from the past, memories of an Italy made up of family ceremonies, communions, confirmations and weddings. Grandpa stuff, we thought. A bit like the doilies on the television and the wedding favors with the music box. Then the gold market came to remind us of a truth: the yellow metal has a much longer memory than ours. At the beginning of the year, gold touched unthinkable levels, exceeding 5,500 dollars an ounce. Silver also experienced an extraordinary run, reaching above 116 dollars. Now the wind has changed: gold has fallen to around 4,100 dollars an ounce and silver has plummeted towards 61 dollars. An important slowdown, but not enough to erase an impressive growth story. Because ten years ago the yellow metal was trading around 30-32 euros per gram. Today we are around 116 euros per gram for the pure one. In short, that hair-thin chain that seemed like a gift of no great importance could today have a value capable of paying a few bills or a few tanks of petrol. In short, the aunt with the white hair and the impeccable skirt perhaps had understood everything before the Wall Street analysts. The great revenge of gold concerns above all those objects that have remained forgotten for decades. Baptism necklaces. Milan knitted bracelets. Earrings passed down from mother to daughter. Those pins with initials that seemed destined to lie forever inside a jewelry box. Today those little pieces of family have a new life. Gold does not need software updates, does not fear hackers, does not require complicated passwords. It doesn’t need artificial intelligence to remind us of its value. He sits there, still, maybe for twenty years, patiently waiting for someone to notice him. And it’s not just the jewels. There is an entire universe of coins that has rediscovered a second youth. The pound, that currency that grandparents bought “for safety”, is today worth around 850-900 euros. A small disc of precious metal which for many seemed just a whim for nostalgic collectors and which today can instead be transformed into a cruise or a nice paid bill. Then there is the Marengo, the 20 franc or 20 lire coin that smells of Napoleonic history. Today its value is around 700 euros. And even the old 500 lire silver Caravelle, the ones with Christopher Columbus’ ships pushed by the wind, have regained their dignity. Common examples are worth around ten euros, but the very rare 1957 version with the “against the wind” flags, which never came into circulation due to the error in the minting, can reach collector’s figures of up to thousands of euros: from 3 thousand to 12 thousand. A sort of “Gronchi Rosa” of Italian numismatics given that the sails are inflated by the wind in the opposite direction to the bow. In short, while technology promises us a future made up of augmented reality and virtual worlds, the past hidden in drawers continues to produce real value. Now this hidden wealth finds a new home: the stock market. The protagonist is Gens Aurea, European leader in regenerated gold, owner of brands such as Orocash, GioiaPura and Luxury Zone. The company became the protagonist of the first major IPO on Piazza Affari after about three years. An important signal: the market is once again looking for true industrial stories, even when they arise from an ancient sector like that of gold. The operation aims to value the group at around 1.4 billion euros and represents a strategic step to accompany international growth. Gens Aurea is not simply an advanced gold buyer. It is an integrated platform that buys used precious stones, recovers them, refines them and returns them to the jewelery supply chain. The group has over 530 stores in Europe and in 2025 recorded 836 million euros in revenues, 105 million in adjusted Ebitda and 68 million in net profit. The objectives are even more ambitious: 1.5 billion in revenues, over 200 million in gross margin and more than 130 million in net profit are expected for 2026. The industrial plan envisages reaching over 750 stores by 2029, with strong expansion in Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Poland and Romania. CEO Fabio Godano summarizes the challenge thus: «We have built a unique platform in the European gold and precious objects market, becoming the largest operator in the regenerated gold sector in Europe. Our platform integrates a widespread presence in retail, industrial expertise, digital skills and rigorous compliance monitoring.” For Godano, the listing represents a natural step to support growth: «We have a plan for 300 new stores in the next three years. A significant portion of our growth will come from our ability to open stores quickly and efficiently.” In short, the future also depends on being able to transform grandmother’s old jewel into a new raw material. The other side of the coin is called Kruso Kapital. Here gold is used as collateral to obtain liquidity. The company was founded in 2017 when Banca Sistema entered the pawn credit sector with the ProntoPegno brand. The goal was to completely change the perception of an ancient activity, often associated with difficult moments in life. The modern version of the pawnshop instead becomes a financial tool for families. In 2022 comes the change of name and a new strategy: to enhance not only jewelery and watches, but also works of art and collectibles. Kruso Art is born, with the acquisition of the Art-Rite auction house, while the Art-Kredit project paves the way for loans guaranteed by works of art. Growth becomes international: Italy, Greece and Portugal. In 2024 the company acquired Pignus, a historic Portuguese pawnbroker. After listing on EGM in 2024, Kruso Kapital made the leap to the main market in 2026. CEO Giuseppe Gentile has explained several times that pawn credit should not be considered an emergency product, but a modern financial service. No longer “I wear the ring because I’m in difficulty”, but “I enhance an asset that I own without having to sell it”. On the occasion of the transition to the main list, Gentile defined the operation: «A natural evolution of the company’s path, destined to increase transparency, visibility and credibility towards investors and customers». In the end the moral is simple. While the world rushes towards cryptocurrencies, artificial intelligence and virtual realities, Italians are rediscovering an ancient heritage. The real national sovereign wealth fund is not hidden in large financial databases. It’s in the drawers with the laundry. Inside those forgotten boxes where a farsighted grandmother had placed a necklace, a coin, a bracelet. Small objects, often considered outdated, which today become protagonists again. Because gold can go down, it can correct, it can take a break. But it has a quality that few investments possess: it knows how to wait. And sometimes, after years of gathering dust, it reminds us of how much it is worth. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Mykhailo Fedorov released a video on Tuesday in which he called for wartime elections. Photograph: Mykhailo Fedorov/Reuters View image in fullscreen Mykhailo Fedorov released a video on Tuesday in which he called for wartime elections. Photograph: Mykhailo Fedorov/Reuters Ukraine Analysis Sacking turns former Zelenskyy loyalist into potent political opponent Luke Harding Mykhailo Fedorov’s blistering critique comes at a time of growing pressure for democratic renewal in Ukraine Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.52 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 13.35 EDT Share For more than a month, demonstrators have gathered in Ivan Franko Square outside Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office. The protesters have been chanting a name – not that of Ukraine’s embattled president but that of the man he recently sacked as defence minister , Mykhailo Fedorov. On Sunday evening, 2,000 people marched along Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s main boulevard, waving cardboard banners in support of their ousted hero. Zelenskyy has refused to reinstate Fedorov, who during his six months in the job was widely seen as an effective and reforming figure. On Wednesday, Ukraine’s parliament, the Rada, voted to approve a successor as defence minister, Yevhen Khmara. The move shows that Fedorov has been shut out from government permanently, and confirms his transition from trusted insider and Zelenskyy loyalist to a potent political opponent. On Tuesday, Fedorov released on YouTube a bombshell nine-minute video . In it, the 35-year-old called for wartime elections and reminded Zelenskyy, his former boss, that power ultimately resided with the people. “Democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia,” Fedorov said. “We must find a legal, safe and ‌realistic mechanism which will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of ​a long war.” Fedorov offered a blistering critique of Zelenskyy’s administration. The country was facing a “systemic crisis of governance”, he said , in which corruption inside the defence ministry was hurting the war effort. Reforms were stymied, loyalists promoted. “The old system lives by its own rules too often. ⁠It protects itself. It is scared of change,” he said, hinting that his own attempts to root out corruption in procurement had led to his sacking. View image in fullscreen A soldier holds a sign reading ‘Fedorov only’ during a protest in Kyiv on Wednesday. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian Most civil society activists agree with this big-picture analysis. Corruption has always existed in Ukraine, in common with other countries that were once a part of the Soviet Union, including and especially Russia. During the 2010-14 presidency of Viktor Yanukovych, who was backed by the Kremlin, it reached spectacular levels. In the peaceful past, large-scale theft from the state budget left less money for schools and hospitals. As Fedorov noted, today’s schemes have “an entirely different meaning” as full-scale war rages. They represent drones not bought, “ammunition that did not reach the front” and technology that “could have been put into production but wasn’t”. The video shows a photo of Andriy Yermak, Zelenskyy’s former chief of staff, who resigned last year amid a corruption scandal implicating other senior figures such as Timur Mindich, Zelenskyy’s former business partner. Yermak’s lawyer has dismissed the allegations as “baseless” and Mindich, who fled to Israel, also denies wrongdoing. Orysia Lutsevych , the deputy director of the Russia and Eurasia programme and head of the Ukraine forum at Chatham House, said of Fedorov’s comments: “I think he’s right. He says the system is old-fashioned, does not run fast enough, stalls innovation and prioritises loyalty.” She said “personal and vested interests” sometimes influenced official decision making, not always in Ukraine’s interests. “This could be called corruption,” she added. At the same time, Ukrainian society – led by students, veterans, journalists and anti-corruption bodies – is politically engaged. “The street is a check on the president. It corrects,” Lutsevych said. “Parliamentarians are active too. Ukraine is a pluralistic space. There are checks and balances even under martial law.” However, she said “nervous exhaustion” and Zelenskyy’s failure to explain his actions had created a public crisis. “It’s a perfect powder box,” she observed. View image in fullscreen A banner at a march in central Kyiv on Sunday. Photograph: Serhii Okunev/AFP/Getty Images Zelenskyy has not yet responded to Fedorov’s accusations. On Wednesday he fired his deputy chief of staff , Iryna Mudra, after the National Anti-Corruption Bureau carried out a raid on her office. The bureau said Mudra and a Rada deputy were suspected of money laundering to the tune of $3.4m. A year ago, Zelenskyy triggered protests when he tried to strip the bureau of its independence. He reversed course after criticism from activists at home and pressure from Kyiv’s European partners. Olena Tregub , a co-founder of the Independent Defence Anti-Corruption Commission, said those “from the system” frequently occupied top posts, at the expense of talented professionals. “Corruption is the symptom. It’s not the cause. The cause of the problem is bad governance,” she said. There were “shades of grey” when it came to military contracts. Outside bodies that monitored procurement were often able to stop dubious purchases, she pointed out. There is little prospect Zelenskyy will hold an election any time soon, or embrace Fedorov’s idea of voting by smartphone. Under Ukraine’s constitution, polls cannot take place during wartime. Nonetheless, pressure for some form of democratic renewal is growing. It could include consultations with government critics and a restless civil society. And when presidential elections are eventually held, Fedorov has nimbly positioned himself to challenge Zelenskyy. https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: France and Germany abandoned the future combat air system project in June. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters View image in fullscreen France and Germany abandoned the future combat air system project in June. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters Aerospace industry Europe’s fighter jet plans are in disarray. What happens next? While the UK and Italy are making progress, France and Germany’s joint venture came to nothing, and the prospect of more countries pulling together seems way off Jasper Jolly Tue 8 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 03.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google W hen the former European Central Bank president and Italian prime minister Mario Draghi laid out a plan for Europe to catch up economically with the US and China, collaborating on defence was one of the prescriptions. No more should each country in Europe try to make its own version of a boat, tank or jet but instead share costs and technologies between allies. Europe appears to have fallen at the first hurdle. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, were forced to cancel the joint future combat air system in June, after fraught efforts to work together since 2018. The question exercising defence executives over the summer since then is: what happens now? France appears to be content to push ahead with its own fighter jet but Germany has been left questioning whether it will have its own aircraft. It may instead be left as a secondary customer to the rival Tempest jet under the global combat air programme (GCAP) led by the UK, Italy and Japan. Meanwhile, in the UK the debate over the summer has been over the future of military spending, after the resignation of John Healey as defence secretary in June over spending commitments, his return under Andy Burnham as chancellor and continued questions over when the UK will meet its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence. Militaries are racing to develop the sixth generation of fighters since the first jets that flew in the second world war. The Tempest and the US’s F47 will be developed to dominate the air, with AI technologies, more advanced stealth and swarms of drones to fly alongside. (The F47 is named , at least until a Democratic president enters the White House, after Donald Trump, the 47th US president.) France and Germany’s effort foundered amid arguments between France’s Dassault Aviation and the Germany-headquartered Airbus Defence and Space over who would lead the programme. France also reportedly wanted a smaller jet capable of landing on its aircraft carriers, while Germany does not have any aircraft carriers. View image in fullscreen Scale models from the now-cancelled future combat air system project. Photograph: Charles Platiau/Reuters The final nail in the coffin came last week, with the French engine maker Safran’s announcement it will end its joint effort to make engines for the fighter jet with Germany’s MTU Aero Engines. A European defence chief executive recently acknowledged that it was not impossible for there to be as many as three European fighter jets if Germany were to try to build one (possibly with partners) to rival GCAP and France . “It would not be ideal,” the boss said, slightly abashed. Three is too many, according to pretty much anyone without a financial interest in winning work share. “No way we end up with three,” one UK-based consultant who works with many of the big prime manufacturers said. “There’s no order book for it. You need an order book to make these economical.” The same person believes that it is unlikely that there will even be two European fighters, given the strained economics. Fighter jet programmes are considered a success in industrial terms if they can make hundreds – about 600 is seen as a good benchmark. That is far beyond the size of any single European air force. France has 228 Rafale fighter jets in service, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies, a thinktank. Dassault is determined to press on. Éric Trappier, the chief executive of Dassault Aviation, last month said a next-generation combat jet could be developed solely in France or in cooperation with other partners. He wants a demonstrator to be flying as early as 2031. The outlines of the story are already familiar to many in the defence industry. In the early 1980s European nations were looking at building a fourth generation of fighter jets. France joined Italy, Spain, West Germany and Britain in a joint effort. Yet disputes over workshare and the capabilities of the final product grew until France walked away. Dassault ended up building the Rafale, while the other four countries are still building the Eurofighter Typhoon 30 years after its first flight. Yet some people are sceptical that Dassault would be able to create something with the same stealth abilities as other sixth-generation jets. Dassault could create a “Rafale plus” or “Super Rafale” with newer radar, weaponry and digital systems, and an upgraded engine, but without a complete redesign to put it at the very cutting edge. The Rafale upgrade already in development for the early 2030s will be able to work in partnership with stealth drones. Another important question – one faced by every air force, including the US and the GCAP partners – is whether a crewed fighter will be outdated by the time it is operating in 2035. However, the consensus in the industry for now appears to be that crewed fighters will still be required, but surrounded by a swarm of “loyal wingmen” drones such as BAE Systems’s Brontanax that can be sent into harm’s way over the horizon by the crewed jet fighter lurking further back. For Germany that leaves the somewhat embarrassing option of asking to join GCAP. Canada joined GCAP at July’s Farnborough airshow but only as an “observer”. That could put it front of the queue to buy products but does not entitle it to the politically valuable manufacturing jobs that come with status as a core partner. (Wealthy Saudi Arabia is also pushing to join , although it does not have much technological knowhow to offer and would be heavily criticised over its human rights record.) “They are very expensive platforms, and having assured orders for them is very helpful,” said Kevin Craven, the chief executive of ADS, the UK aerospace and defence lobby group. “I think there’s a realisation across Europe and Nato that the very expensive platforms require collaboration.” There are “elements of the sixth generation programmes that could work across Europe”, he added. Some of the industrial partners are open to Germany joining. Lorenzo Mariani, the chief executive of Leonardo, Italy’s lead defence company in GCAP, said Germany would be a “positive element” and a “strong financial partner, financially the strongest in Europe”. However, another core partner would add to the risk of delays, he acknowledged. View image in fullscreen An artist’s impression of two next-generation fighter jets flying in the airspace near Mount Fuji in Japan. The UK is developing a jet with Italy and Japan. Photograph: Japanese defence ministry/EPA Reopening discussions to let in another core member could be tricky. The UK, Italy and Japan set up a joint venture called Edgewing to build the Tempest. Marco Zoff, Edgewing’s chief executive, said its aim was “creating the conditions not to fight”. Another insider described it as “having all our fights at the start” over who gets what work, clearing the way for rapid development to be in the air by 2035. Tufan Erginbilgiç, the chief executive of the Tempest jet engine maker Rolls-Royce, told reporters at Farnborough that “I don’t think it will negatively impact GCAP at all” if Germany joins – although he would not be drawn on whether Rolls could share work with MTU. “It is not surprising that more countries are interested, and that will make the programme even more successful because to me it means more markets,” he said. Michael Schoellhorn, the chief executive of Airbus Defence and Space, told reporters in London that the company would join something where they could “have a significant portion of the work and the leadership. That’s currently being explored.” Yet once European executives come back from their summer holidays, they will have to work quickly if they are to avoid the fragmentation that Draghi warned against. Failure to do so would risk repeating the mistakes of the past of building several alternatives that all have to compete against each other for export orders. A European consultant covering the defence industry said: “It would mean we don’t learn.” Explore more on these topics Aerospace industry Europe Manufacturing sector France Germany Airbus features Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story German startup sends first commercial rocket into space from Europe Boeing 737 Max operators told to check fuselages for cracks Airbus to test folding wings for next generation of bestselling planes After fixing its engine problems, Rolls-Royce is turning to its next big challenge SpaceX makes largest ever stock market debut, making Elon Musk world’s first trillionaire France and Germany abandon joint project to build European fighter jet SpaceX targets biggest ever stock market debut, putting Musk on course to be trillionaire Rolls-Royce boss ‘open’ to Germany joining UK’s fighter jet project Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.dw.com/en/at-summit-eu-leade.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OK64 Zelenskyy thanked European leaders for their support in Brussels, saying Ukraine wants to end the war on its country but needs to survive the winter Image: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where leaders from across the bloc pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions. Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine? "This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure." "One ​thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will ​not lift any sanctions unless Russia ⁠stops ​this ​war." The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump 's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions. After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace." Diesel deal between Trump, Putin angers Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that ​they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter." "The winter package is not only energy, ​it's also air defense and funding," he added. During his speech at the summit, Zelenskyy asked European Union leaders to provide an additional €70 billion ($79 billion) in funding to Kyiv next year to help it continue fighting Russia. "The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion euros more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," the Ukrainian president said. When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels. Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran , which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof. "All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace." Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones. Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit. "We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries." Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest. After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing. "I ​assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his ​country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace. The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine. https://english.radio.cz/government-plan.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Government planning to cut ministry staff by 10 percent Facebook Twitter The government will return to a proposal to cut the number of jobs at ministries by 10 percent within the next few weeks, ANO deputy leader and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček said on Czech Television. He said the cuts should not be made in one go, but phased out over the course of next year. Havlíček said the government wants to economize, but stressed that the measures should not affect efficient civil servants or those who are committed to working in public administration. According to Havlíček, an efficient way to reduce staff numbers is to merge organizations. He cited the recent merger of the CzechInvest and CzechTrade agencies as an example, which resulted in around 80 jobs being cut.
